student_passage:
This fictional portrait follows Bea, who looks after a costume cupboard used by several neighbourhood theatre groups. People often imagine that her work consists of hanging clothes in rows. Bea says the harder part is preserving enough information for a garment to be borrowed, used and returned without a new argument at every stage.

The labels originally showed only size and colour. A long coat borrowed for a performance came back with a removable button missing. The next group thought the coat had always been incomplete. (1) ____ Borrowers could compare the garment with that record before taking responsibility for it.

Photographs helped, but they did not explain which changes were allowed. One group wanted to shorten a skirt for a child actor. (2) ____ A temporary fold was acceptable; cutting the fabric was not. Bea made the difference explicit before the scissors appeared, rather than treating a reasonable question as evidence of carelessness.

Some costumes were popular enough to receive overlapping requests. Bea did not settle these by giving the loudest caller priority. (3) ____ When a clash remained, she contacted both groups about alternative dates or garments. A visible arrangement could be discussed; a private favour could not be checked by anyone else.

Near the end of a busy season, she noticed that borrowers regularly arrived after the building's closing time. Repeating the closing hour had not solved the problem. (4) ____ Once the final collection was moved earlier, fewer people were left with a garment they had no agreed way to return that evening.

Bea kept a small notebook of such adjustments. It included rejected ideas as well as rules still in use. (5) ____ A future helper would need to understand why a rule existed before deciding whether a new situation called for a change. The cupboard was organised, but its organisation was never meant to become an unexplained tradition.

共享候选（两项不用）：

A. She told them to cut every garment to the same length.
B. She asked them to use a reversible alteration instead of cutting it.
C. That history helped keep the reasons for decisions available.
D. She replaced every photograph with a list of colours.
E. She began recording each garment’s condition with a dated photograph.
F. She checked whether the agreed collection times left room for the journey back.
G. She used a shared booking record showing when requests had been received.

filled_article:
This fictional portrait follows Bea, who looks after a costume cupboard used by several neighbourhood theatre groups. People often imagine that her work consists of hanging clothes in rows. Bea says the harder part is preserving enough information for a garment to be borrowed, used and returned without a new argument at every stage.

The labels originally showed only size and colour. A long coat borrowed for a performance came back with a removable button missing. The next group thought the coat had always been incomplete. She began recording each garment’s condition with a dated photograph. Borrowers could compare the garment with that record before taking responsibility for it.

Photographs helped, but they did not explain which changes were allowed. One group wanted to shorten a skirt for a child actor. She asked them to use a reversible alteration instead of cutting it. A temporary fold was acceptable; cutting the fabric was not. Bea made the difference explicit before the scissors appeared, rather than treating a reasonable question as evidence of carelessness.

Some costumes were popular enough to receive overlapping requests. Bea did not settle these by giving the loudest caller priority. She used a shared booking record showing when requests had been received. When a clash remained, she contacted both groups about alternative dates or garments. A visible arrangement could be discussed; a private favour could not be checked by anyone else.

Near the end of a busy season, she noticed that borrowers regularly arrived after the building's closing time. Repeating the closing hour had not solved the problem. She checked whether the agreed collection times left room for the journey back. Once the final collection was moved earlier, fewer people were left with a garment they had no agreed way to return that evening.

Bea kept a small notebook of such adjustments. It included rejected ideas as well as rules still in use. That history helped keep the reasons for decisions available. A future helper would need to understand why a rule existed before deciding whether a new situation called for a change. The cupboard was organised, but its organisation was never meant to become an unexplained tradition.
